title: Redwood private VPC security architecture deep dive with Verdant Financial
summary: SE-led deep dive covering Redwood Private (VPC) network design, ingress/egress controls, encryption and key management, RBAC/SSO integration, audit logging and SIEM forwarding. Customer concerned about strict egress controls, KMS/HSM separation, and timeline for SOC 2 evidence. Next steps: share architecture diagram, security whitepaper, and schedule bench test for egress-restricted setup.
next_steps: Redwood to share Private VPC architecture diagram and firewall/NAT configuration notes (Maya)
Send SOC 2 / ISO attestation and security whitepaper (Maya)
Liam to prepare runbook for KMS/HSM integration and key rotation options (Liam)
Customer to provide list of required egress destinations and SIEM endpoint for log forwarding (Aisha)
Schedule follow-up lab to test egress-restricted inference with sample dataset (week of 5/18)
action_items: Maya: email SOC2 report + security whitepaper by 2026-05-10
Liam: produce KMS/HSM integration notes + runbook by 2026-05-12
Verdant (Aisha): share SIEM syslog endpoint and egress allowlist by 2026-05-11
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hi everyone thanks for joining i think we got most people on, quick roll call?
[00:08] Aisha Rahman: hey yes aisha here from verdant, vp engineering.
[00:12] Tom Becker: tom becker, head of security. sorry bit late, had another standup.
[00:17] Liam O'Connor: liam from redwood se, i'll be doing the architecture bits today.
[00:22] Ravi Patel: ravi network arch here, excited to see the ingress details.
[00:26] Maya Chen: great, objective for today is a deep dive on private vpc deployment — network isolation, ingress/egress, firewalling, plus compliance questions, soc2 iso, kms and audit logs. we'll aim for 45 minutes and then open q&a. sound good?
[00:38] Tom Becker: yep that's perfect. main asks: can you run fully air-gapped? how do you handle key material, and what audit logs look like and how long they're retained.
[00:48] Liam O'Connor: good questions. quick high-level: our private offering runs a customer-dedicated control plane in your vpc, optionally with private link endpoints. compute can be in your subnet(s) behind your NACLs and security groups, and we support optional on-prem packages for air-gapped needs. i'll walk through network flow in a moment, but first high level on keys and logs.
[01:05] Maya Chen: before you do, quick note — transcription might show some names wrong, apologies if that happens.
[01:10] Ravi Patel: ha noted.
[01:12] Liam O'Connor: for encryption we support using your KMS — either cloud KMS (aws kms) with customer-managed keys, or an HSM in your environment. keys never leave the customer's KMS; our runtime requests decrypt tokens with an assumed role and never persist plaintext keys. for air-gapped we can integrate with on-prem HSM (PKCS#11) or bring-your-own-HSM models.
[01:34] Tom Becker: when you say never persist, where do ephemeral keys live during runtime — in memory on the GPU hosts? are they swappable if a machine is reprovisioned?
[01:44] Liam O'Connor: yes ephemeral material is in-memory only; we use kernel protections and mlock for critical processes. the KV cache is encrypted at rest; any persisted artifacts are encrypted with the customer KMS key. if a machine is reprovisioned we enforce zeroization procedures, and the orchestration wipes runtime memory and disk. we can share our wipe runbook.
[02:06] Aisha Rahman: that's helpful. on the audit side what do logs look like and how do we forward to our splunk/siem?
[02:13] Liam O'Connor: we emit structured audit logs for control-plane events and for per-request metadata (no model output in control logs). logs can be forwarded to your S3 bucket, to a syslog endpoint, or delivered via private link to your SIEM. retention is configurable; default is 90 days in the console but for enterprise we can push to your long-term archive. all logs include request ids, user ids, role context for RBAC.
[02:36] Tom Becker: do those logs contain any PII or model output by default?
[02:40] Liam O'Connor: important point — by default we do not log model outputs. you can enable request-body logging for debugging but that's opt-in and we recommend redaction. PII should be redacted client-side.
[02:52] Ravi Patel: switching to networking please — show the architecture diagram if you can.
[02:57] Liam O'Connor: sure i'm going to share a quick slide, apologies if the auto transcripter labels this weirdly, but imagine three tiers: control plane endpoints (private link or managed in-customer subnet), inference compute pools in private subnets, and optional rated NAT/egress gateway. ingress is via private endpoints or aws privatelink / azure private link — no public internet required.
[03:18] Maya Chen: (interrupting) quick note on terminology: we often say control plane can be either hosted by redwood in a customer-dedicated account or deployed to your VPC depending on contract.
[03:28] Tom Becker: can you confirm whether we can force all egress to go through our firewall stack? we have strict egress rules and only allow traffic to a handful of vendor IPs.
[03:36] Liam O'Connor: yes, the compute runs in your subnets so you control the route tables and NATs. typical pattern: put inference hosts in private subnets with route table pointing to your egress bastion/NAT gateway which then goes through your FW (palo alto, fortinet, etc). we also support VPC endpoints for s3 and kinesis to avoid public egress when forwarding logs.
[03:58] Ravi Patel: what about ephemeral pulls to get model artifacts — those need to happen at startup. can that be cached internally? we can't open wide egress on the fabric.
[04:06] Liam O'Connor: good catch. we support a pre-warm/cache layer — you can have an internal artifact repo (s3 or artifactory) and we can pull models from your private bucket using VPC endpoint. for managed model catalog we can mirror artifacts into your bucket as part of onboarding, avoiding outbound internet.
[04:22] Aisha Rahman: and for live model updates — how do you handle version pinning and rollback without external calls?
[04:28] Liam O'Connor: we push manifests into your control plane and compute checks the manifest in your internal store. rollouts are orchestrated by your control plane agent; if you want fully offline operations we can schedule maintenance windows to pull updated artifacts from an air-gapped transfer.
[04:44] Tom Becker: ok that helps. two compliance questions: can you provide attestation for SOC2 + iso 27001 and do you have a list of encryption algorithms and ciphers used in transit?
[04:55] Maya Chen: we'll send our SOC 2 and ISO reports — currently we have SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 certs for our hosted and dedicated offerings; for private deployments we provide the same evidence and operational runbooks. cipher list — we publish TLS 1.2+ with AEAD ciphers (TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, etc) and you can mandate TLS 1.3 only if you like. we'll include the crypto spec in the packet.
[05:18] Ravi Patel: about identity — we use okta and want SAML + SCIM for provisioning and RBAC. how do you integrate?
[05:24] Liam O'Connor: we support SAML 2.0 SSO and SCIM v2 for user provisioning. roles are mapped to RBAC roles inside the console; you can map groups to roles like admin, eng, auditor. for API keys we have short-lived tokens and recommend using OIDC or mTLS for service-to-service auth.
[05:42] Tom Becker: do you have support for FIPS 140-2 HSMs? our compliance team asks.
[05:47] Liam O'Connor: we support FIPS-validated HSMs in BYOK mode — if you bring an HSM we can integrate via PKCS#11. we also integrate with cloud HSM offerings that are FIPS compliant.
[05:58] Aisha Rahman: logging and monitoring — i want to ensure we can correlate model request traces with our app traces in jaeger/datadog.
[06:05] Liam O'Connor: we emit trace ids and support open telemetry headers. you can forward traces to your tracing backend via a private collector — we can push request traces (metadata only) to your datadog ingestion endpoint or internal tracing system.
[06:20] Maya Chen: quick pause — any blockers so far or red flags from verdant security?
[06:25] Tom Becker: primary concerns are egress allowlist, key custody clear steps for HSM integration, and ability to get raw audit logs to our SIEM with guaranteed delivery. also want clarity on data residency in our eu region.
[06:36] Liam O'Connor: for egress allowlist we support static egress IPs from managed outbound gateways if you use our managed NAT — but if you require all traffic to be within your egress stack you can run compute entirely in your account and then we don't use our NAT.
[06:51] Ravi Patel: about firewalling — do you expect any inbound rules to be opened on our perimeter? we're strict about inbound.
[06:57] Liam O'Connor: inbound is limited to private link endpoints or peering. we don't require opening inbound internet ports. for management plane agents we use outbound connections that are authenticated and can be proxied through your bastion if needed.
[07:12] Aisha Rahman: what about patching and OS-level hardening — do we manage the hosts or do you?
[07:17] Liam O'Connor: if compute is in your account you manage OS patching and AMI hardening; we supply hardened images and a recommended CIS benchmark. if using Redwood-managed compute we handle patching and provide CVE reports and maintenance windows. both models have tradeoffs.
[07:33] Tom Becker: on retention — can we set audit logs to 7 years? our legal asked for long-term retention for certain records.
[07:39] Liam O'Connor: yes if logs are delivered to your archive bucket we can support any retention you configure on your side. our default console retention is shorter but enterprise configs allow archive to S3 Glacier or equivalent.
[07:52] Maya Chen: i'm going to call out a few product features that help with cost and security: model quantization profiles are done during build and are stored as artifacts; there's no cross-tenant leakage. we also have automatic token-level redaction options for logs.
[08:08] Ravi Patel: how do you handle network segmentation for multi-tenant clusters if we choose dedicated pool?
[08:13] Liam O'Connor: dedicated pools are single-tenant by customer id. if you pick dedicated capacity it's isolated at the hypervisor level and logically segmented; for strictest isolation we recommend private deployment in your VPC or on-prem.
[08:26] Tom Becker: can we get an architectural diagram showing the path of a request from our app to the model and back including ports, subnets, and firewall rules?
[08:33] Maya Chen: yes we'll attach that — liam will export a detailed diagram and a recommended firewall ruleset.
[08:38] Liam O'Connor: (typing) i'll include required ports: control plane 443 to private endpoint, s3/vpc endpoints for artifact pulls, optional ssh to bastion for debug — but we prefer agent-based ephemeral sessions.
[08:51] Ravi Patel: do you have IDS/IPS integration? we use palo alto and a cloud ngfw.
[08:55] Liam O'Connor: we can integrate with your NGFW and IDS. traffic flows through your firewall stack when compute is in your account. for managed deployments we support TAP/flow logs and can forward telemetry to your monitoring tools.
[09:07] Aisha Rahman: any specifics about lateral movement protections — e.g., if one inference node is compromised can it touch our internal db subnets?
[09:16] Liam O'Connor: we recommend strict subnet segmentation and security groups that enforce least privilege. by default compute subnets do not have db access; any necessary access should be via narrow API endpoints with mTLS. we also support fine-grained IAM roles and temporary credentials for any service integrations.
[09:34] Tom Becker: timeline question — if we wanted private vpc deployment with on-prem HSM and SIEM integration, what is typical lead time?
[09:42] Maya Chen: for standard private VPC it's 4-6 weeks including network setup and onboarding. adding on-prem HSM and SOC-specific artifacts typically extends to 8-12 weeks depending on procurement and access schedules.
[09:55] Ravi Patel: will you need direct access to our environment for initial setup?
[09:59] Liam O'Connor: we usually work through an install runbook — we need an IAM role with limited permissions to write to your s3 repo and launch cloud resources if you opt for us to provision. alternatively we provide terraform modules for you to run with our guidance. all access is timeboxed and audited.
[10:15] Aisha Rahman: regarding data residency — our eu workloads must stay in eu-west-1. can you guarantee model artifacts and inference data remain in region?
[10:24] Liam O'Connor: yes region pinning is supported. compute and artifact storage can be restricted to the region; logs and backups can be pushed to your regional archive. we'll include region mapping in the architecture doc.
[10:38] Tom Becker: ok last set of questions — do you have drift detection for config and policy? e.g., terraform drift and security group changes?
[10:45] Liam O'Connor: we integrate with config management tooling and can push alerts to your ticketing system. we also provide an optional policy engine that watches for changes and can auto-remediate or alert based on severity.
[10:57] Maya Chen: great, let's move to wrap up. any open items we didn't capture?
[11:02] Tom Becker: want to see the wipe/zeroization runbook and confirm FIPS HSM integration steps.
[11:07] Ravi Patel: i'll send the exact egress allowlist and SIEM endpoints.
[11:10] Aisha Rahman: please include estimated cost delta for running everything in our account vs redwood-managed, especially egress/nat costs.
[11:18] Maya Chen: noted — we'll include cost delta and recommended approach.
[11:22] Liam O'Connor: quick recap of next step items: i'll produce the detailed vpc diagram and firewall rules, soc2+iso docs will be emailed, and we'll set up a lab run with egress-restricted test.
[11:32] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the lab, speak soon.
[11:36] Aisha Rahman: thanks all.
[11:38] (call ends)
